items.prompt: `isDue(state, now)` returns `state.attempts > 0 && new Date(state.dueAt) <= now`. A refactor drops the `attempts > 0` part because "the date comparison is enough". What breaks?
items.answer: Every unseen card becomes due, because emptyCardState stores dueAt as the 1970 epoch
distractors: Nothing: an unseen card stores a null dueAt, and `new Date(null) <= now` evaluates to false
Only cards answered wrongly become due early, because their dueAt is set ten minutes out
Mastered cards stop coming due, because the attempts counter is what pushes them into review
items.explanation: An unanswered card needs some dueAt in a NOT NULL column; the epoch was chosen as "long ago". The attempts guard and that default are one decision split across two files: change either alone and every unseen card counts as due.

items.prompt: At the baseline (6f1bf43), a learner drills a module and answers the same card correctly twice, 60 seconds apart. What does the scheduler do, and why?
items.answer: It masters the card after 60 seconds, since schedule never read state.dueAt, so spacing was not enforced
distractors: It rejects the second answer with a 409, because the card is not due again until local midnight tomorrow
It counts the second answer as a lapse, because answering before the due date resets the card's reps
It keeps reps at 1, because schedule ignores a correct answer given before the card's dueAt has passed
items.explanation: Behaviour 11: spacing was not enforced, and pickOrdered re-served non-due cards on purpose, so two quick correct answers mastered a card. The self-test even asserted it as a pass.

items.prompt: To stop rep-farming, ADR-0015 makes an early correct answer "practice" (no schedule movement). Why did it reject the simpler rule "require a minimum gap since the last answer"?
items.answer: Any minimum gap is arbitrary, and it would block the 10-minute relearn after a lapse
distractors: A minimum gap needs a new database column, and the schema had no migration mechanism
A minimum gap would let a replayed POST double the XP, which the practice rule prevents
A minimum gap cannot be tested deterministically because the clock is not injectable
items.explanation: Alternatives rejected: a minimum gap is arbitrary and blocks the 10-minute relearn after a lapse. Keying on dueAt reuses the schedule the card already has.

items.prompt: After ADR-0015, a card answered at 10:00 with a 1-day interval gets dueAt = local midnight starting tomorrow, not now + 24 h. What goes wrong if dueAt were kept to the millisecond?
items.answer: Studying a bit earlier tomorrow, say 09:55, would earn practice instead of a rep on a card shown as due
distractors: Cards that come due exactly at midnight would be served twice within the same daily review session, doubling XP
Intervals longer than 180 days would overflow the ISO date string that dueAt is stored as
A wrong answer could no longer bring the card back for a relearn ten minutes later
items.explanation: "Due to the millisecond" was rejected because it turns "back in 1 day" into practice for anyone who studies earlier than yesterday. startOfLocalDay uses calendar arithmetic so the rule also holds across DST.

items.prompt: A fresh card (ease 2.5) is answered correctly on time three times. What are ease and intervalDays afterwards, and why that interval?
items.answer: ease 2.8 and intervalDays 8: the third interval is round(3 x 2.8), using the already-raised ease
distractors: ease 2.7 and intervalDays 8: ease only moves after the first interval has elapsed
ease 2.8 and intervalDays 7: the third interval is round(3 x 2.5), using the ease from before the answer
ease 2.5 and intervalDays 9: ease is fixed until a lapse and the interval triples each time
items.explanation: The multiplier is next.ease, not state.ease. Three correct answers raise ease by 0.3 to the 2.8 cap, and round(3 * 2.8) = 8. On-time answers then run 1, 3, 8, 22, 62, 174, 487 days without a cap.

items.prompt: Which wrong answer increments `lapses`: the very first answer to a new card being wrong, or a wrong answer after the card already had one correct rep? Why the distinction?
items.answer: Only the wrong answer after a correct rep; missing a new question the first time is not forgetting
distractors: Both, because every wrong answer resets reps to zero and is recorded as a lapse on the card
Only the first-ever wrong answer, because later misses are recorded under the 'failed' outcome instead
Neither: lapses only grows when a mastered card (reps >= 2) is missed after its due date
items.explanation: next.lapses = state.lapses + (state.reps > 0 ? 1 : 0). A lapse requires a card that had been learned; the outcome for an unlearned miss is 'failed'.

items.prompt: ADR-0002 grades on the server. A teammate proposes shipping a hashed answer to the browser so grading works offline. Why was that alternative rejected?
items.answer: A multiple-choice key has so few possible values that its hash is brute-forced by trying each choice
distractors: Browsers have no built-in hash function, so the key would need a crypto library shipped in the bundle
Hashing is slow on low-end phones, so every answer would lag while the browser compared the hashes
The hash would change whenever the explanation text was edited, breaking every stored attempt
items.explanation: Alternatives rejected: "The hash of a four-way choice is brute-forced by trying four values." A small answer space makes hashing worthless as secrecy.

items.prompt: The server strips `answer` before sending a question, yet "always press 2" scored 93%. What leaked, and what was the fix?
items.answer: The key's position: choices went out in authored order, key mostly at index 1; ADR-0014 shuffles per serve, grades by id
distractors: The key's value: the explanation text named the right choice; the fix was to strip the why text before sending it
The key's length: the right choice was usually the longest; the fix was padding every choice to the same length
Response timing: correct answers came back faster; the fix was a constant-time grader with a fixed delay
items.explanation: The decision protected the key's value and ignored its position: the key was index 1 in 363 of 389 mcq/output questions (M-01). Shuffling per serve plus grading by choice id removes the tell.

items.prompt: What does server-side grading cost the product, and what does the ADR say an offline mode would need instead of shipping the key?
items.answer: Every answer is a round trip, so there is no offline mode; offline would need signed, deferred grading
distractors: Grading becomes CPU-bound on the server; an offline mode would need a worker thread for every learner
Answers can no longer be explained; an offline mode would need the why texts cached in localStorage
Choices can no longer be shuffled; an offline mode would need a seeded shuffle shared with the client
items.explanation: Consequences: "every answer is a round trip, so there is no offline mode". Revisit when: an offline mode is required, then the client needs signed, deferred grading, not the key.

items.prompt: ADR-0009 keeps a trimmed SM-2 and rejects FSRS even though FSRS predicts retention better. What is the stated reason?
items.answer: FSRS needs parameters fitted from review logs, which the app does not have yet
distractors: FSRS requires a 0-5 self-rating after every answer, which adds a slow decision per card
FSRS cannot represent the 10-minute relearn step that follows a wrong answer
FSRS is licensed for non-commercial use, so it cannot ship inside this app
items.explanation: Alternatives rejected: FSRS "needs parameters fitted from review logs this app does not yet have". The ADR also notes elapsedMs and answered_at are already stored so constants can be fitted later.

items.prompt: Real SM-2 asks for a 0-5 quality grade after each answer. Why does this app map every correct answer to quality "good" instead of asking the learner?
items.answer: A quiz only sees right or wrong, so a self-rating adds a per-card decision for a signal it can't give honestly
distractors: Storing a 0-5 grade per answer would need a schema migration that the attempts table could not take safely
Self-ratings would let learners inflate their XP by always choosing 5, so the server ignores them
SM-2's quality grade applies only to cloze cards, so it has no meaning for multiple-choice questions
items.explanation: Context: a quiz has only right or wrong, and asking learners to self-rate would slow every card. Rejected alternative: one extra decision per card, for a signal a multiple-choice answer cannot give honestly.

items.prompt: In the working tree, the third-and-later interval is `Math.max(1, Math.min(MAX_INTERVAL_DAYS, Math.round(state.intervalDays * next.ease)))`. What breaks without the `Math.max(1, ...)` floor?
items.answer: An imported card with reps >= 2 and intervalDays 0 gets 0 days, so it is due before the answer, forever
distractors: A card with a very low ease would get a negative interval and stay scheduled in the past for ever after
Cards answered just before midnight would be scheduled for the same day and counted twice in that session
The 180-day cap would be bypassed for any card whose ease reached the 2.8 maximum and kept growing
items.explanation: The comment: a state that arrived through import can carry reps >= 2 with intervalDays 0, and 0 * ease would put the card due at today's midnight, before this answer, so it never leaves due.

items.prompt: After the practice rule shipped, learners who had farmed repeated answers saw their XP drop once at upgrade, with no migration touching an XP column. Why?
items.answer: XP is not stored; it is replayed from the attempt log via schedule(), so old repeats re-score as practice
distractors: The upgrade migration deleted attempts that were recorded before their card's due date, taking their XP
XP is cached per session, and that cache was invalidated when the new outcome field was added to attempts
The 365-day replay window introduced with the rule cut the farmed attempts out of the XP total
items.explanation: Because XP is replayed from the log (ADR-0004 as amended by J14), learners who farmed repeats before this change see their XP drop once. replayXp reuses schedule() so practice earns 1 for history too.

items.prompt: Why not fix rep-farming by simply never serving a card before it is due?
items.answer: It removes practice from drills, and the API could still be called directly to farm reps
distractors: Daily sessions would run out of due cards and start returning fewer questions than requested
The client caches questions, so it would keep showing non-due cards even after the server stopped
It would make the 10-minute relearn impossible, because relearn cards never count as due
items.explanation: Rejected: never serving non-due cards removes practice and still leaves the API able to farm reps. The fix has to live in schedule(), where every answer passes.

items.front: F-01 at baseline: the self-test passes, yet "two spaced correct answers" is false. Which check pinned the bug, and what was the fix?
items.back: check.js called schedule(state, true, now) twice with the same now and asserted mastery. J10/ADR-0015: a correct answer before dueAt is practice and leaves reps, ease and dueAt alone.

items.front: M-02: grade() returns { correct: false } for a malformed response such as "1" instead of 1. What did the route then do, and what was the fix?
items.back: It recorded the attempt, scheduled a lapse and revealed the key. J09 rejects it as 400 invalid_response before recording anything.

items.front: Baseline scheduler, on-time correct answers: intervals 1, 3, 8, 22, 62, 174, ... What was missing, and what else made cards clump?
items.back: No maximum interval (the next step is 487 days); the contract caps it at 180 (MAX_INTERVAL_DAYS). No jitter either, so cards learned together come due together.

items.front: Where does the "due at local start of day" rule break first?
items.back: Learners in several time zones on one server: local start of day is the server's zone. Revisit when learners say an answer did not count on a card the UI showed as due.
